title: “UNCOVER NAKEDNESS”: The Disturbing Phrase in Leviticus 18 We Were Never Supposed to Read Casually
paragraphs: “UNCOVER NAKEDNESS”: The Disturbing Phrase in Leviticus 18 We Were Never Supposed to Read Casually
Why does God repeatedly use this strange expression for forbidden sexual relations—and what does an ancient Hebrew phrase reveal about sex, boundaries, shame, holiness, and the grace of Jesus Christ?
There are phrases in the Bible we read too quickly because slowing down would make us uncomfortable.
This is one of them.
“Uncover nakedness.”
Again.
And again.
And again.
Leviticus 18 repeats the expression so often that eventually you have to stop and ask:
Why?
Why not simply say, “Do not have sex with this person”?
Why speak of nakedness?
Why describe sexual violation as something being uncovered?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
What if this ancient expression is exposing something about us too?
Not merely about bodies.
Not merely about sexuality.
But about what human beings do when desire stops listening to God.
Because buried inside Leviticus 18 is a truth our generation desperately needs to recover:
Not everything you desire belongs to you.
Not every intimacy you can pursue is yours to take.
Not every boundary that frustrates you exists to imprison you.
And sometimes what the world calls liberation, God recognizes as destruction.
Listen to the Hebrew.
Leviticus 18:6 says:
אִישׁ אִישׁ אֶל־כָּל־שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ לֹא תִקְרְבוּ לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה אֲנִי יְהוָה
Ish ish el-kol she’er besaro lo tiqrevu legalot ‘ervah, ani YHWH.
In a fairly literal rendering:
“No one shall approach any close relative of his flesh to uncover nakedness. I am YHWH.”
The crucial Hebrew expression is:
לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה — legalot ‘ervah
“To uncover nakedness.”
The verb comes from גלה — galah, carrying the basic idea of uncovering, revealing, exposing, or making something no longer concealed.
The noun עֶרְוָה — ‘ervah refers to nakedness, especially exposed sexual nakedness or the private parts, with nuances depending on context.
Put them together in Leviticus 18 and we encounter a Hebrew sexual expression whose meaning becomes unmistakable from the laws surrounding it.
This is not merely a prohibition against accidentally seeing somebody without clothing.
The chapter is establishing boundaries around sexual access.
That becomes particularly clear because Leviticus itself changes its vocabulary when necessary.

For example, after repeatedly saying “uncover nakedness,” verse 20 addresses adultery using different and more explicit sexual language. Verses 22 and 23 likewise use other expressions for prohibited sexual acts. The chapter therefore does not depend upon one euphemism alone. Its surrounding language establishes that the subject is prohibited sexual relations.
And that matters.
Because if we reduce “uncover nakedness” to simply “seeing someone naked,” we miss the force of the passage.

One scholarly explanation describes the expression as a euphemistic way of speaking about sexual intercourse, although interpreters debate some of the phrase's precise lexical and relational nuances in individual verses.
So we should be careful.
We should not pretend every linguistic question surrounding עֶרְוָה has been solved.
But neither should uncertainty about some details erase what the chapter plainly does.
Leviticus 18 draws sexual boundaries.
And God takes those boundaries seriously.
Why?
Because biblical sexuality is never merely about bodies touching.
It involves covenant.
Kinship.
Faithfulness.
Vulnerability.
Trust.
Consequences.
Another person's dignity.
And ultimately, obedience to the God who created the body in the first place.
That is where this strange phrase becomes hauntingly beautiful.
“Uncover nakedness.”
Because nakedness is vulnerability.
When someone becomes naked before another person, something normally concealed becomes exposed.
Defenses disappear.
Privacy disappears.
Something guarded becomes accessible.
Sexual intimacy therefore reaches into territory far deeper than appetite.
Scripture begins its story of human sexuality not with shame, but with astonishing innocence:
“The man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.”
Genesis 2:25.
Think about that.
Naked.
Yet unashamed.
Known.
Yet safe.
Exposed.
Yet not exploited.
Vulnerable.
Yet not violated.
That was the garden.
Then sin entered.
And one of the first things humanity noticed was nakedness.
The man and woman covered themselves.
They hid.
And when God called, Adam answered that he was afraid because he was naked.
Something had changed.
The human body had not suddenly become evil.
Sexuality had not suddenly become evil.
Marriage had not suddenly become evil.
But sin had entered the human experience, and what had once existed without shame was now surrounded by fear, hiding, domination, blame, lust, exploitation, and broken trust.
That makes Leviticus 18 far more than an ancient list of people Israelites were forbidden to sleep with.
God is teaching His people that sexuality requires boundaries because human desire, after the Fall, cannot safely appoint itself as its own god.
Read the chapter carefully.
God repeatedly says:
אֲנִי יְהוָה — Ani YHWH.
“I am the LORD.”
That is the heartbeat beneath the prohibitions.
God does not merely say, “Don't.”
He reminds Israel:
“I am your God.”
Leviticus 18 opens by warning Israel not to pattern itself after Egypt, where they had lived, or Canaan, where they were going. Instead, God's people were to walk according to His statutes.
In other words:
Your culture does not get the final word about your body.
Your appetite does not get the final word.
Your trauma does not get the final word.
Your loneliness does not get the final word.
Your hormones do not get the final word.
Pornography does not get the final word.
Your secret messages do not get the final word.
The person telling you, “If it feels right, it must be right,” does not get the final word.
Ani YHWH.
“I am the LORD.”
And suddenly Leviticus 18 stops feeling ancient.
Because we live in a world obsessed with uncovering.
We uncover bodies for entertainment.
We uncover ourselves for validation.
We consume other people's nakedness through screens.
We reduce people bearing the image of God to pixels.
We call lust private because nobody else is physically standing in the room.
We maintain secret conversations we would panic to see projected onto the church wall.
We flirt with people who belong to someone else.
We rationalize emotional affairs because “nothing physical happened.”
We cross boundaries slowly enough that we can pretend we never crossed them.
And sometimes we do something even more dangerous.
We use grace to excuse what Jesus died to free us from.
Maybe that sentence hurt.
Stay with it.
Because this article was never written merely to explain Hebrew.
It was written for the person reading this with something hidden.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your pastor doesn't know.
Your family doesn't know.
Your friends at church would never suspect it.
You know exactly how to worship.
Exactly when to raise your hands.
Exactly what Christian words to use.
Exactly what Bible verse to post.
But there is another version of you that appears when the door closes.
Another browser history.
Another conversation.
Another appetite.
Another relationship.
Another fantasy.
Another compromise.
Another secret.
And somewhere along the way, you became exhausted from protecting the image of a person you know you are not consistently living as.
This is where people often misunderstand holiness.
We imagine God standing outside the bedroom because He hates pleasure.
Scripture presents something far richer.
The God who established sexual boundaries is the same God who created male and female.
The same God who established marriage.
The same God whose Scriptures can celebrate marital desire.
The same God who invented the human capacity for intimacy before humanity invented pornography, adultery, exploitation, abuse, or sexual shame.
God is not anti-sex.
He is against what destroys His good purposes for it.
Boundaries are not evidence that something has no value.
Often boundaries exist precisely because something has enormous value.
We put fences around dangerous cliffs.
We place priceless things behind protection.
We make covenants around promises too important to treat casually.
And God surrounds sexual intimacy with moral boundaries because bodies are not disposable.
People are not products.
Vulnerability is not merchandise.
And another person's nakedness is not simply something your desire has the right to possess.
But now comes the question that can terrify anyone who has already crossed the boundary:
What about me?
What about what I already did?
What about the affair?
What about the pornography?
What about the relationship?
What about the years of compromise?
What about the sexual choices I cannot undo?
What about what somebody did to me?
Here we must make a distinction that Christians sometimes tragically fail to make.
Being sexually sinned against is not the same as committing sexual sin.
If someone violated, abused, assaulted, manipulated, coerced, groomed, or exploited you, their sin is not transferred onto you as moral guilt.
Your wounds may be real.
Your confusion may be real.
Your grief may be real.
Your healing may take time.
But another person's evil does not make you spiritually filthy beyond the reach of Christ.
Jesus is not disgusted by the wounded person coming to Him for mercy.
And for the person who has sinned sexually, Scripture does not tell you to pretend it was nothing.
Grace does something much more powerful.
Grace allows you to call darkness darkness without believing darkness gets the last word.
That is repentance.
Not self-hatred.
Not religious theater.
Not posting enough Bible verses to drown out conviction.
Repentance is agreeing with God strongly enough to turn.
And Christianity makes an outrageous announcement to guilty people:
Your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
Paul wrote to believers in Corinth after listing patterns of serious sin, including sexual sin, and then said something staggering:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because they became morally perfect overnight.
Not because consequences magically disappeared.
Not because sin suddenly stopped mattering.
But because something happened to them.
Paul continues:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
—1 Corinthians 6:11
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
That is the Gospel.
Christianity is not the story of clean people avoiding dirty people.
It is the story of a holy Christ rescuing sinners.
Jesus does not rewrite our scandal by pretending it never happened.
He rewrites it by entering the story with a cross.
The cross tells the truth about sin more brutally than our excuses ever will.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
But the cross also tells the truth about grace more beautifully than our shame ever could.
God's mercy is so astonishing that Christ willingly went there for sinners.
At the cross, holiness and mercy do not cancel each other.
They meet.
Justice is not shrugged away.
Grace is not sentimentalized.
Christ bears sin.
The guilty are offered forgiveness.
The ashamed are invited out of hiding.
The enslaved can begin walking toward freedom.
And the person whispering, “If everyone knew what I had done, nobody could love me,” encounters a Savior who already knows.
Completely.
And still calls sinners to come.
But come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come without bargaining.
Come without editing the story.
Come without renaming sin so repentance becomes unnecessary.
Jesus said:
“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.”
Then He said:
“I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.”
Mark 2:17.
The Great Physician cannot heal the version of you that you keep insisting is not sick.
Bring Him the real wound.
Bring Him the real addiction.
Bring Him the real relationship.
Bring Him the real browser history.
Bring Him the real memories.
Bring Him the secret you keep trying to bury beneath Christian appearances.
Bring Him what you are ashamed to name.
Christ already knows what is underneath the covering.
And He still calls you toward the light.
Maybe this is why the language of Leviticus feels so piercing.
Human beings have spent thousands of years uncovering what God told us not to uncover...
while desperately covering what God is calling us to confess.
We expose bodies.
Then hide souls.
We reveal skin.
Then conceal sin.
We crave intimacy.
Then fear being truly known.
And Jesus walks directly into that contradiction.
Not carrying a camera to humiliate you.
Not carrying gossip to destroy you.
Carrying scars.
The hands reaching toward repentant sinners are wounded hands.
The Savior calling you out of darkness is the Savior who was stripped, mocked, wounded, publicly humiliated, and crucified.
He knows shame.
Yet He had no sin of His own to confess.
He bore ours.
And because He rose from the grave, shame does not get resurrection power over those who belong to Him.
Your past can explain some of your scars.
It does not have the authority to become your god.
Your temptation can describe a battle.
It does not have the authority to define your identity.
Your failure can become part of your testimony.
It does not have to become your destiny.
So perhaps the question after reading Leviticus 18 is no longer merely:
“What does ‘uncover nakedness’ mean?”
Perhaps another question has quietly appeared.
What have I been uncovering that God told me to guard—and what have I been hiding that Jesus is asking me to bring into His light?
Do not answer that publicly unless wisdom says you should.
But answer God.
Honestly.
Tonight.

If necessary, seek mature pastoral accountability. If there is addiction, pursue serious help. If there is an adulterous relationship, stop romanticizing what repentance requires. If pornography owns part of your private life, stop negotiating with it. If your marriage is wounded, pursue truth, wisdom, repentance, counseling, and restoration where restoration is safely possible.
And if you have been abused or exploited, please hear this carefully:
You do not need to repent for another person's crime against you.
Seek safety.
Seek wise support.
Tell someone trustworthy.
Healing is not betrayal of your faith.
Truth is not shameful.
What happened to you does not make you untouchable to Christ.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for wounded people.
There is also room there for repentant guilty people.
That is what makes grace scandalous.
Nobody gets to boast.
We come needing Christ.
If this exposed something hidden in your life, you don't have to tell strangers the details.
If Christ has already been restoring areas of your life you once thought were beyond redemption, tell someone else there is hope.
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed to read tonight.
And please don't let this message die on your screen.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Someone may be drowning in pornography.
Someone may be considering adultery.
Someone may carry years of sexual shame.
Someone may believe Jesus could forgive everybody except them.
Someone may have been violated and still wrongly believes the shame belongs to them.
Leviticus 18 is not the kind of passage most Christians understand after one hurried reading.
It doesn't.
It can't.
And not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces the giving, generosity, service, and stewardship God may call you to practice through your local church and toward people in need.
It doesn't.
Scripture says Christian giving should be purposeful and voluntary—“not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That means support should come from worship, not spiritual pressure.
Your support helps the work continue.
Your sharing helps the message travel.
Your prayers matter.
And your participation can help put biblical truth in front of another human being at exactly the moment they need it.
Leviticus 18 teaches us that holiness has boundaries.
The cross teaches us that boundary-breakers can be forgiven.
And the resurrection teaches us that forgiven people do not have to remain what they were.
Maybe your story contains scandal.
Maybe it contains sexual failure.
Maybe betrayal.
Maybe addiction.
Maybe abuse.
Maybe years of hiding.
Maybe consequences you cannot reverse.
The Gospel never promises that every earthly consequence disappears.
It promises something greater:

Jesus Christ can take a sinner who finally stops hiding, wash what guilt has stained, begin transforming what sin has distorted, and write grace into places shame insisted could never become holy again.
So bring Him the chapter you wish you could tear out.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the wound.
Bring Him the desire.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him you.
Because perhaps the most dangerous nakedness was never an uncovered body.
Perhaps it is a soul standing completely exposed before a holy God with nowhere left to hide.
And perhaps the greatest miracle is discovering that the sinner who runs to Jesus in repentance does not find a Savior waiting to exploit that exposure...
but a Savior who already bore the shame of the cross to cover the repentant sinner in a righteousness that could never be earned.
You may remember the moment your scandal was exposed—but eternity will remember the Savior who refused to let your scandal have the final sentence.
